​ @Aunt_Ducky 

There's a clear wrap cover, too. These are typically called fresh rolls or summer rolls. And you're more likely to find them at a Vietnamese, Thai, or pan-Asian place, not Chinese. I don't think I've ever seen the clear Fresh rolls at a Chinese restaurant. 

Spring rolls have a thin, crispy shell and are traditionally vegetarian, filled with cabbage and other veggies. Although today they can have meat in them, too. They are dipped in a sweet sauce and culturally eaten in the early spring for good luck. 

Egg rolls were created in the US with wan ton wrappers when spring roll wrappers weren't available. The wrappers are thicker. They are usually bigger and fatter than a spring roll and can have all kinds of meat and veggie fillings. Neither the filling nor the wrapper has egg, although they are typically about the diameter of an egg. :)

Summer rolls or fresh rolls are filled with salad veggies like lettuce, raw cabbage, grated carrots, and often a piece of shrimp or tofu. The wrapper is clear and stretchy. You often dip them in a peanut sauce.

text:
​ @RoseNZieg ​ I don't know that the material of the wrapper matters -- My reading says both spring and egg roll wrappers are wheat. 

There's a clear wrap cover, too. These are typically called fresh rolls or summer rolls. And you're more likely to find them at a Vietnamese, Thai, or pan-Asian place, not Chinese. I don't think I've ever seen the clear Fresh rolls at a Chinese restaurant. 

Spring rolls have a thin, crispy shell and are traditionally vegetarian, filled with cabbage and other veggies. Although today they can have meat in them, too. They are dipped in a sweet sauce and culturally eaten in the early spring for good luck. 

Egg rolls were created in the US with wan ton wrappers when spring roll wrappers weren't available. The wrappers are thicker. They are usually bigger and fatter than a spring roll and can have all kinds of meat and veggie fillings. Neither the filling nor the wrapper has egg, although they are typically about the diameter of an egg. :)

Summer rolls or fresh rolls are filled with salad veggies like lettuce, raw cabbage, grated carrots, and often a piece of shrimp or tofu. The wrapper is clear and stretchy. You often dip them in a peanut sauce.

Here is the history of the Chinese in the USA:   The first Chinese individuals arrived in the U.S. in the late 1780s to early 1800s as sailors, merchants, and ship workers, with government records noting arrivals starting around 1820. Large-scale immigration began later.

Early Arrivals (Late 1700s–1830s)

• 1784–1785: Trade ties opened via the Empress of China, bringing a small number of Chinese sailors and cooks to U.S. ports (like New York and Baltimore).
• 1815: A small trickle of Chinese merchants and former sailors arrived.
• 1834: Afong Moy arrived, widely noted as the first Chinese woman in the U.S.
• 1820: U.S. federal records begin tracking small numbers of Chinese arrivals (roughly 325 men before 1849).

The Gold Rush Wave (Late 1840s–1850s)

• 1848–1849: The California Gold Rush drew the first large wave of laborers and fortune-seekers ("Gold Mountain").
• 1850s: Numbers grew rapidly; Chinese workers mined gold, farmed, and worked in fisheries and early factories.

Major Milestones

• 1860s: Thousands of Chinese laborers built the Transcontinental Railroad. Basically from the West cost East and other labors coming from Europe built the railroad from the East to the West until the two parts met.

Slushie is not Chinese. Not even American Chinese. May be a restaurant gimmick. But not Chinese by any stretch. 

Americanized Chinese food is not authentic Chinese, and neither is Britishized Chinese Food. But at many American Chinese restaurants (not Panda Express, but places in your city's international district), you can get genuine Chinese, often on a separate menu you have to ask for. If there are Chinese people eating in the restaurant, that's a good sign. The genuine dishes tend to put off Americans. Like chicken feet. Dishes with textures that USAmericans don't tend to like. And organ meats and spice profiles we find unusual and most are iffy about trying. 

General Tso's is distinctly Americanized Chinese. Invented in the US and named for an imaginary general. 

I have seen Britishized Chinese on YouTube. The "spice bag", that's totally British and I don't understand what it is and why it's called that. Nobody in the US has ever heard of a "spice bag" at a Chinese restaurant. 

Orange chicken is similar to sweet and sour, but not the same. There are other dishes with the same consistency, too. Fried chunks of chicken with a warm sauce poured over. The sauce tends to come separate if it's carry-out, so the food doesn't get soggy. Sweet and sour sauce can be bright pink or brown, depending on whether they use the bright food coloring or not. Orange sauce is more dark orange and flavored like oranges. General Tso's and Sesame or Honey Sesame chicken are also a similar consistency, but the sauces are sticky and don't come separate. Tso's can be somewhat sweet and/or spicy, while Sesame is more sweet and light and comes with lots of Sesame seeds on. 

And chips/fries make ZERO sense with Chinese food. At least Americanized Chinese is the same type of food as authentic Chinese, just with flavors slanted a bit more toward the USAmerican palate and some veggies made local. Chips are just a British favorite that you've decided to add to Chinese food and... then act as if it was Chinese?? That's outright bizarre. 

We do often have burgers and fries and chicken strips at our ethnic restaurants, but we don't pretend those are ethnic foods. They'll be under a separate menu heading as "American food" or even just listed with the children's menu, and are there in case one person in your party doesn't like ethnic food or can't eat without having something super familiar. Typical of children or some neurodivergent people. 

So it's like early Chinese restaurateurs in England realized right off that the English simply can't eat dinner at all without their chips, so they added chips to the menu at Chinese restaurants, even though those are about as far as you can come from Chinese food. "Father, we're but seeking anything here unless it comes with chips." "Well, Mother, then I guess we're selling chips. I guess we'll learn how to make those now!"
